node.label: Quebec historiography
node.period_rationale: Period 1 (c. 1945–70) is when Quebec historiography professionalizes into university schools: the IHAF (1946) and RHAF (1947), the Montreal and Laval schools in the 1950s–60s. Groulx’s earlier national history is an earlier root in period 0; he is cited by 29 PhDs (2009–26), mostly for his memoirs, as a source. The modernist generation and its critics belong to periods 2 and 3.
node.date_label: Earlier national history (Groulx) · Institut d’histoire de l’Amérique française founded 1946, its Revue from 1947 · Montreal and Laval schools 1950s–60s · Histoire du Québec contemporain 1979 · Rudin’s critique 1992 · coverage through 2000; post-2000 extension partial (Catholic Action revision 2002–05)

date_span.basis: Selected milestones. Groulx’s national history is an earlier root, not a boundary; 1946 is the founding of the IHAF and 1947 the Revue’s first issue, not founding dates for the field; 2000 is the atlas coverage boundary.

node.description: Historical writing on Quebec and French Canada, mostly in French, long organized around the nation, the Conquest of 1760 and the meaning of modernity. Lionel Groulx’s national history of French Canada closes what a francophone anthology calls the time of the ‘ancients’; Groulx founded the Institut d’histoire de l’Amérique française (1946) and its Revue (1947). In the 1950s historians at Montréal (Séguin, Frégault, Brunet) made the Conquest and its consequences their central problem. At Laval, Trudel wrote the history of New France, and Hamelin and Ouellet economic and social history, Ouellet in a conjunctural idiom indebted to Labrousse. Their agricultural-crisis thesis (1962) was contested by Paquet and Wallot (1972–73); Dechêne, trained in the Annales milieu in France, wrote the social history of seventeenth-century Montreal (1974). After 1970 a modernist generation turned to contemporary, urban and industrial Quebec and to its whole population (Linteau, Durocher and Robert, 1979). Women’s history followed, from the Collectif Clio (1982) to Baillargeon (1991); Lévesque (1997) asked how far colleagues had integrated it. Behiels (1985) found the Quiet Revolution’s prelude in 1945–60; Rouillard (1997) recorded a shift from reading it as rupture to turn. Ronald Rudin (1992, 1997) argued that the modernists’ search for a ‘normal’ society muted religion, rurality and ethnicity; Linteau and Fecteau replied (1995). Bouchard and Lamonde (2000) close the period; after 2000, Meunier and Warren, Bienvenue and Gauvreau traced the Quiet Revolution to Catholic Action.
node.scope_note: A research field defined by its object (Quebec and French Canada) and largely by its language. The Montreal school, Laval, the modernists and their critics are distinct and overlapping positions, not one school; Savard warns against treating ‘École de Québec’ as a unit. The post-1970 generation is called ‘modernist’ after Bédard and Goyette’s part title; Linteau calls it a ‘nouvelle histoire’; Rudin’s polemical name for it is used only in the normal-society debate strand. Annales influence is indirect and contested: Ouellet’s Labroussian economic history, Mandrou’s preface and Dechêne’s training in the Annales milieu are documented, while Linteau says his generation owed more to sociology and American historians. Groulx’s nationalism and clerical politics are historical subjects here, not the atlas’s categories. Quebec women’s history (Clio, Lévesque, Baillargeon) and the Catholic Action revision of the Quiet Revolution have their primary homes here. English-language historians of Quebec (Behiels, Dickinson, Young, Rudin, Greer) belong to the field. Acadian and francophone-minority historiography outside Quebec is only touched by Martel. New France encounter history with Indigenous peoples is in native_newcomer.

strands.title: Groulx and French-Canadian national history
strands.focus: Groulx’s national history and his conception of history. Groulx founded the Institut d’histoire de l’Amérique française in 1946 and its Revue in 1947, and wrote in its first issue. The anthology places him at the end of ‘le temps des Anciens’.
strands.works: Histoire du Canada français depuis la découverte (1950); IHAF (1946); RHAF 1:1 (1947)

strands.title: The Montreal school and the Conquest
strands.focus: Séguin, Frégault and Brunet make the Conquest and its economic and national consequences their central problem (titles); Savard groups them by shared ideological outlook.
strands.works: Séguin (thesis 1947; 1970); Frégault, La guerre de la Conquête (1955); Brunet, La présence anglaise et les Canadiens (1958)

strands.title: Laval: economic and social history
strands.focus: Trudel’s history of New France and of slavery in French Canada; Hamelin and Ouellet’s economic and social history of New France and Lower Canada. Savard notes Ouellet’s debt to Labrousse and Chaunu, and Mandrou prefaces his 1966 book. Savard treats Trudel and Ouellet as distinct despite the label ‘École de Québec’.
strands.works: Trudel, L’esclavage au Canada français (1960), Histoire de la Nouvelle-France (1963–); Hamelin, Économie et société en Nouvelle-France (1960); Ouellet, Histoire économique et sociale du Québec (1966)

strands.title: The Lower Canadian agricultural crisis debate
strands.focus: Ouellet and Hamelin’s 1962 agricultural-crisis thesis and Paquet and Wallot’s 1972–73 counter-interpretation, with Wallot’s Quebec ‘qui bougeait’. A dated exchange; titles only.
strands.works: Ouellet and Hamelin (1962); Paquet and Wallot (1972, 1973); Wallot (1973)

strands.title: New France as social history
strands.focus: Dechêne’s habitants and merchants of seventeenth-century Montreal, from a Paris doctorate (1973) after training in the Annales milieu of Mandrou and Goubert; Hamelin’s economy and society of New France.

strands.title: The modernist synthesis
strands.focus: Linteau describes his generation’s turn to c. 1850–present, to urban and industrial Quebec, and to the history of Quebec’s whole population rather than French Canadians alone; social history and serial sources, with Annales influence filtered through sociology and American history. Histoire du Québec contemporain and Dickinson and Young’s Short History are its syntheses.
strands.works: Linteau, Durocher and Robert (1979; 1986); Linteau (1983); Dickinson and Young (1993 ed.)

strands.title: Quebec women’s history
strands.focus: Collectif Clio’s four-century history (1982), Lévesque’s norms and “deviant” women (1989), Baillargeon’s Depression housewives (1991) and her short synthesis (2012). Lévesque (1997) judged that women’s history had redefined traditional Quebec history while some colleagues were slow to integrate women. The anthology places Clio and Micheline Dumont in its modernist part. Primary here (Q38): 31 of 34 PhDs citing this literature engage Quebec historiography; cdn_women_gender keeps its critique edge (cwg_rel_03). The Collectif Clio (1982) was Micheline Dumont, Michèle Jean, Marie Lavigne and Jennifer Stoddart; shared methods or positions are not inferred.

strands.title: Origins of the Quiet Revolution: rupture or turn?
strands.focus: Behiels finds the Quiet Revolution’s prelude in 1945–60 liberal and neo-nationalist debate (1985); Rouillard records historians’ shift from ‘rupture’ to ‘tournant’ (1997). The Catholic Action strand extends the argument after 2000.
strands.works: Behiels (1985); Rouillard, “La Révolution tranquille: rupture ou tournant?” (1997)

strands.title: Catholic Action and the Quiet Revolution
strands.focus: Against the Quiet Revolution’s own story of a clerical “grande noirceur”, Catholic Action, personalism and lay movements from the 1930s are read as preparing the 1960s. Two versions (Baum): social democracy (Meunier and Warren) and the family and gender (Gauvreau). Gauvreau judged that Quebec religious history had repeated the Quiet Revolution’s own ideology until these studies. Post-2000 extension; moved from cdn_religion_reform (Q12): 75 of 85 PhDs citing this literature engage Quebec historiography (lift 5.6), 36 of them at francophone universities.

strands.title: The ‘normal society’ debate
strands.focus: Rudin argues that the revisionists’ normal, Western Quebec muted religion, rurality and ethnicity (1992; 1995; 1997). Linteau and Fecteau reply in the Bulletin d’histoire politique (1995), and Fecteau reviews Rudin’s book on nationhood and the “revisionist school” (CHR 1999). A named controversy with dated published contributions.

strands.title: Quebec historians on their historiography
strands.focus: Savard’s quarter-century survey (1974), Serge Gagnon on Quebec historians from Garneau to Groulx (1978), Rudin (1997), and Bédard and Goyette’s anthology (2006), whose four parts give a francophone periodization.
strands.works: Savard (1974); Gagnon (1978); Rudin (1997); Bédard and Goyette, eds. (2006)

strands.title: Society, ideas and comparison at the turn of the century
strands.focus: Dumont’s genesis of Quebec society (1993), Bouchard’s Saguenay and comparative New World nations (1996, 2000), Lamonde’s social history of ideas (2000) and Martel on the end of a pan-Canadian French Canada (1997).

extension_coverage.note: Selected post-2000 works only: the Catholic Action revision (Meunier and Warren 2002; Bienvenue 2003; Gauvreau 2005, with reviews 2004–09), moved from cdn_religion_reform; Parole d’historiens (2006); Baillargeon’s synthesis (2012). Létourneau, Bédard and the 2000s debates on national history are not reviewed.

relation_to_periods: Main-period entry across periods 0–3: Groulx as earlier root, professional schools and the IHAF/RHAF in period 1, the modernist generation and women’s history in period 2, the normal-society debate in period 3. Post-2000 selections (the Catholic Action revision 2002–05; Bédard and Goyette 2006; Baillargeon 2012) are extension records.

proposed_relationships.relationship: Labroussian economic and social history at Laval
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Savard (1974) says Ouellet owed a debt to Labrousse and Chaunu; Robert Mandrou prefaced Ouellet’s 1966 book (review heading). Dechêne trained in France in the Annales milieu of Mandrou and Goubert before her Paris doctorate (1973), published as Habitants et marchands (1974) (Charron, Dictionnaire universel des créatrices; formal supervision not asserted). Linteau (1983) says social history began in Quebec in the 1960s under Annales influence but that his generation was shaped more by French and Quebec sociologists and American historians. Specific contributions to the Laval and New France strands, not an Annales origin for Quebec historiography.

proposed_relationships.relationship: The modernist generation adopts social history
proposed_relationships.map_label: New social history and the modernists
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Linteau (1983) describes his cohort adopting social history and serial sources (censuses, civil registers), becoming more quantitative, and widening the subject from French Canadians to Quebec’s whole population. Self-description of one generation.

proposed_relationships.relationship: French-Canadian national history and its revision
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Groulx’s national history and the Montreal school’s Conquest belong to the national-narratives umbrella; Rudin’s opening sets the historians’ ‘normal’ Quebec against both nationalist history and politicians’ distinct society. Comparison only: the field is not reducible to national narrative, and the modernists rejected that frame.

Brunet’s ‘English presence’ and ‘two Canadas’ (1958 subtitle) and the Laurentian national tradition are parallel national historiographies with different subjects and politics. Title-level; the cdn_national_tradition drafter may have a stronger witness (e.g. Berger’s Writing of Canadian History).

Rudin names Rouillard among the historians he criticizes; Rouillard writes the history of Quebec unionism, and Copp and Bradbury write Montreal’s working class (cdn_working_class sources). Overlap in people and subject; no direction asserted. PhD context: 79 PhDs engage both rosters (expected 34.6, lift 2.28).

Rouillard’s ‘turn not rupture’ and the Catholic Action revision (now a strand here) connect this field to religion and secularization. Gauvreau anchors the proposed religion entry, which also proposes the specific contribution crr_rel_04 into the catholic_action_origins strand. Broad comparison; title and abstract level.

proposed_relationships.map_label: Collectif Clio and Quebec women’s history
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Quebec women’s history (Collectif Clio 1982; Lévesque 1989, 1997; Baillargeon 1991, 2012) is primary here (Q38), and its authors also appear in the proposed women and gender entry, which keeps a specific critique edge (cwg_rel_03). Bédard and Goyette place Clio and Micheline Dumont in Quebec historiography’s ‘modernist’ part.

proposed_relationships.relationship: The Quiet Revolution as a Sixties subject
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Rouillard’s abstract makes the early 1960s the contested hinge of Quebec history. Coordination edge with the proposed cdn_sixties entry, which lists quebec_historiography as related; the Sixties drafter may supply stronger evidence (e.g. Mills 2010).
